extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, in-house counsel, and patent practitioners handling Section 101 motions
extracted.subtask_description: Practical procedural and substantive guidance for plaintiffs and defendants on raising, opposing, and structuring 35 U.S.C. § 101 challenges at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage (motion to dismiss), with emphasis on representative claims, pleading specificity, and the Alice two-step framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (Alice two-step)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Alice, the Section 101 analysis proceeds in two parts: Alice Step 1 considers 'whether the claims at issue are directed to … patent-ineligible concepts' (e.g., abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena). If the claims are directed to ineligible subject matter, Alice Step 2 requires a 'search for 'an inventive concept – i.e., an element or combination of elements that is sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself.''
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice Step 1 is generally treated as a question of law resolvable on intrinsic evidence; Alice Step 2 asks whether the claim contains something 'significantly more' than the ineligible concept. Courts apply these steps sequentially; case law (Alice, Mobile Acuity, Simio) should be cited when framing arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raising Section 101 at the motion-to-dismiss stage
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general matter, a defendant may raise a Section 101 challenge on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion where the fact that the patents claim an unpatentable idea, law or phenomenon is apparent on the face of those patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mobile Acuity reiterates that Section 101 may be decided at the pleading stage when the patent's face shows ineligibility. However, whether an affirmative defense like Section 101 can be asserted via a pleading-stage motion is controlled by regional circuit law — parties outside the Ninth Circuit should confirm their circuit's approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff cannot evade a pleading-stage Section 101 challenge by omission
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff may not avoid a motion to dismiss simply by failing to make Section 101-related allegations in the complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Section 101 is an affirmative defense that can be apparent on the patent face, omission of eligibility-related allegations generally won't prevent a defendant from moving to dismiss; plaintiffs may strategically 'embrace' Section 101 by pleading facts that support eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of factual allegations to defeat 12(b)(6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations in the complaint intended to avoid a §101 motion must be specific; conclusory allegations will be disregarded, and allegations unsupported by or that contradict the patent's written description cannot defeat a motion to dismiss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments adding well-pled, specific facts (as in Aatrix) can preclude dismissal; but mere conclusory statements that a claim is unconventional or inventive are insufficient. Cite AI Visualize and Aatrix for examples where courts rejected conclusory pleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing an inventive concept (Alice Step 2) — nonconventionality requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To survive Alice Step 2, the patent must recite an inventive concept that is 'something significantly more' than the abstract idea — i.e., an element or combination that is not conventional, routine, or well-understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an element is conventional can involve questions of fact (Berkheimer). Plaintiffs should plead facts explaining why the claimed features are unconventional; defendants should argue conventionality and show why alleged facts do not preclude dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on the same innovation for both Alice Step 1 and Step 2
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff that argues the same asserted innovation both (a) shows the claim is not directed to an abstract idea at Step 1 and (b) constitutes the inventive concept at Step 2 risks procedural disadvantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the court concludes at Step 1 that the innovation is an abstract idea, the plaintiff cannot then rely on that same concept at Step 2 as the inventive concept. Defendants should look for and exploit this overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric Power principle for computer-implemented inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim that can be reduced to the basic concepts of 'collecting, analyzing, and presenting information using ... conventional operations of generic computer components' cannot survive Section 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting pleadings or responding, parties should map claimed elements to the 'collecting/analyzing/presenting' abstraction to argue ineligibility; plaintiffs should instead allege how the claim improves computer functionality beyond that template.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant's burden and approach when identifying a representative claim
rubrics_metrics.description: If a defendant chooses to identify a representative claim, it must show that the challenged claims 'are 'substantially similar and linked to the same' ineligible concept.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants should be clear and steadfast in explaining why a particular claim(s) is representative because the burden to justify representativeness lies with the defendant. Provide a persuasive, coherent theory tying claims to the same ineligible concept to overcome the presumption of validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's obligations when a defendant identifies a representative claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff cannot simply remain silent; it must provide some explanation to refute a defendant's showing and present at least 'non-frivolous arguments' why the identified representative claim cannot be decisive of all claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs can meet this burden by showing why a claim has 'distinctive significance' that would materially affect the eligibility analysis or by pointing to meaningful claim differences; failure to do so risks invalidation of the entire asserted patent based on a subset of claims (Mobile Acuity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity applies to each claim independently
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim of a patent is presumed valid independently of the validity of the other claims (35 U.S.C. § 282), which informs the burden when arguing representativeness and invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require defendants to justify treating one or a few claims as representative of others because of this statutory presumption; attorneys should address and overcome that presumption in briefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific showing required to justify discovery or claim construction delay
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid dismissal on the ground that claim construction or discovery is needed before resolving Section 101, a patentee must identify specific details supporting that need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentee must do more than 'conclusorily assert[] it needs discovery' — it must propose a specific claim construction and explain why the dispute must be resolved before Section 101 can be decided. Defendants should seek to rebut by showing construction/discovery would be irrelevant or futile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical advice: plaintiffs may plead improvements in computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs may provide robust factual allegations explaining why the claimed invention recites an improvement in computer functionality that goes beyond mere speed and efficiency, or otherwise recites an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such allegations, if specific and consistent with the specification, can strengthen opposition to a 12(b)(6) §101 motion (Aatrix and related cases are examples where amended pleadings avoiding conventionality led to reversal of dismissal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical advice: defendants should highlight plaintiff silence and inconsistencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendants should emphasize where plaintiffs fail to contest representativeness, fail to explain why discovery or claim construction is needed, or fail to clearly explain why claims go beyond an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlighting a plaintiff's silence can support an argument for early, sweeping dismissal; defendants should be prepared to show why asserted gaps justify deciding Section 101 at the pleading stage.
